headline: This law lets federal officials reconsider burial or memorial honors for certain people who may have committed a capital crime but were never convicted, and it directs removal of one named veteran's remains from a Michigan national cemetery.
what_it_does: The law lets the Secretary of Veterans Affairs or the Secretary of the Army review whether a person buried in a national cemetery may have committed a federal or state capital crime, when no conviction happened because the person died or fled to avoid prosecution. If an official finds after a hearing that the person committed the crime, the family or other authorized person gets notice and 60 days to file a disagreement, which starts an appeal. Once the decision is final, remains can be removed or headstones taken down. The law also requires written notice of a conviction before burial or memorialization, instead of before an application is approved. It separately directs the VA to disinter Michael LaShawn Anderson from Fort Custer National Cemetery in Michigan, notify his next of kin, and release the remains to them or arrange other disposition.

who_it_affects.group: Next of kin and others authorized to arrange burial for people buried in national cemeteries
who_it_affects.how: They receive notice of proposed removal of remains or headstones and have 60 days to file a notice of disagreement that starts an appeal.

who_it_affects.group: Michael LaShawn Anderson's next of kin
who_it_affects.how: They must be notified of the planned disinterment and receive the remains, or the VA arranges disposition if the next of kin of record cannot be reached.

who_it_affects.group: Families of people buried or memorialized in the National Cemetery System or Arlington National Cemetery
who_it_affects.how: Their loved ones' burial or memorial status may be reviewed if federal officials receive information about a possible unconvicted capital crime.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 20, 2013; the summary does not give a separate effective date for each provision.
